title: True RSI Isn't Here Yet; The Bottleneck Is Peak Intelligence, Not Compute
dek: Automation inside the labs is concentrated on measurable tasks like software engineering and log monitoring, while scaling laws demand exponential compute for linear intelligence gains — RSI is more likely to make models cheap than to make intelligence explode.
why: Medium information density, but it offers a first-hand counter-framework to the RSI timeline, suited to practitioners who want to calibrate their expectations for AI progress.
who: Founders, investors and engineers tracking the AI progress timeline, especially those who want to calibrate the RSI narrative against the actual degree of automation inside the labs.
skip: Readers uninterested in the timeline prediction table from the Dwarkesh podcast can skip the specific year enumeration around 2:52.

points.h: Anxiety inside the labs is amplified by culture
points.body: The author observes that thousands of concurrent agents are already working continuously inside frontier labs, which rapidly raises employees' expectations for the speed and risk of AI progress. But he argues that the feverish competitive culture of the San Francisco AI scene itself amplifies any AI worry; fear sells, yet it brings second-order negative effects. He recalls the fierce safety debates in 2023 and 2024 about the survival of open-source AI, when the main risks predicted at the time did not arrive on schedule. Jumping from that anxiety to extinction risk, in his view, ‘feels very religious’.

The author cites Richard Ngo's summary: a large portion of the AI safety community is implicitly or explicitly betting on an intelligence explosion within a few years. His own default expectation is that these people will be ‘directionally correct but factually wrong’ — no superintelligence in the next 8 years, but things will move fast enough that the short-timeline camp feels right. He calls this state lossy self-improvement: self-improvement is lossy, not true RSI.

points.h: Scaling inference compute is not RSI
points.body: From the Dwarkesh and Noam Brown podcast, the author realised that the short-term acceleration from large-scale inference capacity is considerable, and labs will throw thousands of agents at important and measurable problems. But he doubts that as total compute rises, labs can necessarily afford to spend a fixed share of compute on internal R&D, especially with IPO plans and scrutiny of basic economics. He stresses not conflating the relatively predictable dynamic of inference-time scaling with the highly uncertain output of RSI.

points.h: Intelligence is jagged; thresholds are discontinuous
points.body: From the three-way discussion between Dwarkesh and John Schulman, Beren Millidge and Charlie O'Neill, the author extracts a key problem: discussions of RSI lack a clear definition of ‘intelligence’. The jaggedness of intelligence means one must discuss thresholds on specific measurable tasks. The shape of LLM intelligence is very different from humans, yet the roles we predict are human-shaped, so AI will not cross thresholds discretely like a remote worker or an AI researcher, but will diffuse slowly, with a long tail forever.

points.h: The scientific bottleneck is understanding, not experiments
points.body: The author thinks many people underestimate the communication and standard-building-with-colleagues part of science. He believes the loop of experiment design and testing will be 10x faster in the near future, but does not believe hypothesis generation and intuition building will be. Accelerating understanding is the key bottleneck, and despite major improvements in AI tools, human ability here will only improve marginally. A great advance in science is letting humans spend more time here, not making humans exponentially stronger at it.

The author points out that when it comes to improving AI models, RSI helps efficiency more than it scales peak intelligence. The reason is that LLM serving has clear, measurable, malleable metrics to improve, which brings better inference-time scaling and more efficient multi-agent systems. But all scaling laws show that linear intelligence gains require exponential compute and resources. RSI will make modern LLMs dramatically cheaper, and the trend of exponentially falling cost at a fixed intelligence level may accelerate. For labs the key is improving margins, and the Jevons paradox will likely prevail, bringing a strong business.

The author quotes John Schulman: post-training teams need many people because there are many different domains to figure out how the model should behave, and it is hard to automate the whole thing because someone always has to think about how the model should behave in this domain. Schulman also said post-training is easy to screw up in ways a given benchmark cannot see. The author agrees these tasks are especially hard for current LLMs, and although it will get better as RL environments scale rapidly, this paradigm will not last forever, and building and testing new environments that can truly challenge leading LLMs may become exponentially harder in the future.

points.h: Automation inside the labs is concentrated on routine tasks
points.body: The author read the internal RSI measurements shared by OpenAI and Anthropic, and his reading is: the biggest takeoff in internal lab automation is concentrated on fairly routine but not always simple tasks like software engineering, monitoring logs, and managing planned experiments. He was especially surprised by the wording in the Claude Fable 5.1 & Mythos 5.1 system card: internal use of recent AI models is a key factor in maintaining the current pace of progress, but no clear signs of acceleration beyond that pace have yet been seen. The author concludes that the hardest exponent to push is peak intelligence, and early RSI is more like scaling inference-time compute massively and diffusing it into AI research and related activities, with plenty of low-hanging fruit remaining.

terms.def: An AI system that can autonomously improve its own intelligence, forming an accelerating loop.
The author's alternative concept: AI can accelerate parts of the process, but information and understanding are lost in transmission, so full RSI cannot form.
AI capability is uneven across tasks rather than improving smoothly as a whole.
Efficiency gains lower unit cost, which instead increases total demand and total consumption.
